Senator Beebe Center, Representative Hasenfus and distinguished members of the Criminal Justice and Public Safety Committee:
My name is Jan Collins, I am Assistant Director of Maine Prisoner Advocacy Coalition (MPAC) an organization committed to ethical, positive, and humane changes in Maine's prison system. I am speaking in support of LD 1980 An Act to Implement the Recommendations of the Stakeholder Group to Examine and Improve the Recruitment, Retention and Wellness of Law Enforcement Officers.
The health and wellness of first responders, including corrections officers, law enforcement, EMS and public safety dispatchers are essential to their ability to fulfill the responsibilities of serving the community.
As a member of the Franklin County Board of Visitors, retention and recruitment is a major concern and a priority area for us to address. It is a central area of our annual report. High turnover does not benefit anyone. Not the employer, the officers or the people they serve. Anything that we can do to increase longevity is a positive.
We are very proud of Franklin County's Sargent Close and his work around the state on first responder wellness. First responder positions are punctuated by high levels of stress. Centering mental health in the curriculum is essential to increasing longevity in these positions. but it is also essential to individual lives.
Corrections officers and first responders, have high levels of divorce suicide and shortened life spans. We must invest in the people who put their lives on the line as an indication that we value their work and their lives.

I believe that this bill applied to all first responders has a very reasonable price tag.
We must invest in the people who invest their lives in us.
Thank-you, Jan Jan M. Collins Assistant Director Maine Prisoner Advocacy Coalition

Statement in support of
L.D. 1980, An Act to Implement the Recommendations of the Stakeholder Group to Examine and Improve the Recruitment, Retention and Wellness of Law Enforcement
Officers
Joint Standing Committee on Criminal Justice and Public Safety
January 12, 2026
Senator Beebe-Center, Representative Hasenfus, and honorable members of the Criminal Justice and Public Safety Committee. My name is Scott Stewart. I am the Chief of the Brunswick Police Department, and the president of the Maine Chiefs of Police Association. I am providing testimony on behalf of the Association in support of LD 1980.
The Maine Chiefs of Police Association's mission is straightforward: to strengthen the working relationships among Maine's police leaders, to promote professionalism and consistent standards across the state, and to support the men and women who serve our communities every day. At the heart of that mission is a shared commitment to protecting life and property and upholding the values of our profession.
For those of us who lead law enforcement agencies, the wellbeing of our officers is always at the front of our minds. We prepare them for difficult situations, we try to shield them from unnecessary harm, and we do everything we can to make sure they go home safely at the end of each shift. But policing is demanding work. It takes a toll, and that toll has made it harder to keep experienced officers and to bring new people into the profession.
The stakeholder group that the Legislature created took these challenges seriously, and we appreciate the thoughtful work that went into its recommendations. LD 1980 is the followthrough that puts those ideas into practice in ways that will genuinely help officers and the communities they serve.
We are especially encouraged to see the creation of a Law Enforcement Retention Advisory Council, and we appreciate that the Maine Chiefs will have a voice in that work. Chiefs see the

daytoday realities of recruitment and retention, and we are ready to contribute to longterm solutions.
We also support the bill's efforts to strengthen officer wellness. Recognizing first responders on death certificates, improving wellness and criticalincident debriefing training at the Maine Criminal Justice Academy, and funding a statewide Wellness Coordinator are all meaningful steps. These policies will directly affect the health, resilience, and longevity of the people who show up for Maine's communities every day.
LD 1980 is a practical, thoughtful bill that helps address the challenges facing law enforcement across the state. On behalf of the Maine Chiefs of Police Association, I respectfully urge you to support it.
Thank you for your time and consideration.

Senator Beebe-Center, Representative Hasenfus, and members of the Criminal Justice and

Public Safety Committee, my name is Tanya Emery, and I am providing testimony today in support

of LD 1980 at the direction of the

fimcipal Association's (MMA) Legislative Policy

Committee (LPC). MMA is a nonpartisan, nonprofit member service organization that aims to help

provide policy solutions that work for all residents of Maine. The LPC is composed of 70

municipal officials from across Maine, elected by their peers to represent member communities.

-

LD 1980 is a critical step in supporting Maine's law enforcement officers and their

families. The report of the Stakeholder Group on Law Enforcement Recruitment, Retention, and

Wellness documented the tremendous difficulty that agencies face trying to recruit new officers at

a rate that offsets attrition. The work of the group confirmed these challenges around recruitment,

retention, and wellness are systemic, statewide problems, not isolated challenges. Law

enforcement officers (LEOs) are asking for wellness programming and support, while retirees are
shedding light on the long-term impact of LEO service. The stakeholder report provides clear,

actionable recommendations focused on "higher order needs" such as department culture,
'
opportunities for advancement, and a sense of support and belonging.

MMA supports LD 1980 as it provides clear, evidence-based recommendations to address recruitment, retention," and wellness challenges among the LEO community. MMA itself
recognized the need forsupport and resources and in 2024 rolled out ServeStrong, a confidential
mental health and trauma-based service for first responders and their families via a 24/7 web
platform, in partnership with National League of Cities Risk Information Sharing Consortium.
This free resource includes professional mental health assessments, trauma-based telehealth
therapy, and other resources tailored specifically to the needs of the LEO community. The mental
health and wellbeing of first responders is a top priority for our communities and therefore for
MMA.

MMA urges the committee to support LD 1980 and stands ready to collaborate with state

and local partners to establish a sustainable framework for implementing and funding these

important recommendations. Building a reliable, affordable system that law enforcement officers

and their families can trust is essential. Thank you for your time and attention to this matter, and I

am happy to answer any questions you might have.

.

RE: LD1980 - An Act to Implement the Recommendations of the Stakeholder Group to Examine and Improve the Recruitment, Retention and Wellness of Law Enforcement Officers
Senator Beebe-Center, Representative Hasenfus, and Distinguished Legislative Members of the Criminal Justice and Public Safety Committee;
My name is William Doyle. Currently I serve in the role of Executive Director for the National Correctional Employees Unions (NCEU). The National Correctional Employees Union (NCEU) represents nine (9) County Correctional Units in the State of Maine comprising of approx. five hundred (500) members from York to Aroostook County. We have been advocating for correctional, communication, and law enforcement officer salaries and benefits since 2010 in the State of Maine.
The NCEU would like to thank the Sponsor Senator Beebe-Center for your efforts and support for the law enforcement community. The NCEU wholeheartedly supports this legislation implementing the recommendations of the stakeholder group, with some recommended amendments.
Sec. 3., 2-H. - Training regarding officer wellness. - ADD the Basic Corrections training program
Chpt. 415, �3891, Sub-Sec. 2 Membership - ADD an individual representing the National Correctional Employees Union
The recommendations being presented are reasonable and support former rebuttable presumption legislation recognizing Post Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) as a reason for disability. The challenges our LEO's face daily accumulates over time, especially during the course of a career. From car wrecks to hanging attempts, our LEO's see traumatic events at a greater rate than non-first responder careers. A 2012 national study of nearly 3,000 correctional officers and staff conducted by Caterina Spinaris, Ph.D. with Desert Waters Outreach in Colorado found a 27% PTSD rate among all correctional staff and a depression rate of 26%. Among security personnel the rate is 34%, substantially higher than the general population and all other first responders. A wellness program designed to educate and provide healthy coping mechanisms for law enforcement officers will help reduce workplace errors and disciplinary actions.
But with the abundance of employment options paying similarly, the evolving Maine Criminal Justice Academy Standards, and general lack of stable scheduling, it's becoming increasingly more difficult to attract and retain correctional and other first responder personnel. The NCEU, FOP, MAP, and other agencies have recently encountered some issues at the Maine Criminal Justice Academy, where these aforementioned standards are challenging employment norms and undermining collective bargaining. While the previous legislature's thought process of allowing the MCJA rulemaking authority was to enhance the law enforcement profession, the result is more alarming and eventually going to exacerbate current staffing shortages.
In closing, the NCEU would like to reiterate our support for LD1980 and urge the committee and full legislature pass this important piece of legislation. Thank you very much for your time and I'm happy to answer any questions.
In Solidarity,

William Doyle Executive Director
